Ambassadors at a Round Table

Graph TheoryAlgorithmsCounting
Game: Ambassadors sit round a table, and some of them are enemies (red lines). Win by seating them so that nobody sits next to an enemy.
How to play: Press one ambassador, then another: everyone from the first to the second, going round the table, is turned around. The Hint button shows a good turn.

<
Look for the math

If 2n ambassadors are invited and each has at most n−1 enemies, they can always be seated round a table so that nobody sits next to an enemy. The picture turns the problem into a graph: the ambassadors are dots, enemies are joined by red lines, and you want a circle through every dot that uses no red line.

An algorithm, not just a proof

Seat them any way, and count the pairs of enemy neighbours. Take one such pair, A then B. Walk on from B and look for a pair of neighbours B′, A′ where B′ is not an enemy of A and A′ is not an enemy of B. Turn the whole arc from B to B′ over: now A sits beside B′ and B beside A′, and the number of enemy neighbours has dropped by at least one. The Hint button does exactly this.

Why the lucky pair exists

A has at most n−1 enemies, so at least n friends, and those friends have n neighbours on one side. B has at most n−1 enemies, so one of those neighbours must be a friend of B. The logic test did not take this on trust: for every graph on 4 and on 6 ambassadors in which nobody has more than n−1 enemies, and every seating, the lucky pair existed and each use of it lowered the count; the same held for 40,000 random graphs at the limit of the condition with up to 30 ambassadors.

Sufficient, not necessary

The condition is not needed for a good seating: draw every diagonal and no side of a regular polygon, and each ambassador has far more than n−1 enemies, yet nobody sits next to one. Without it there may be no seating at all: if one ambassador is everyone’s enemy, he always sits between two others.

The applet draws its enemies at random, each ambassador picking a quarter of the others; that does not promise the condition, so some boards have no solution, and the Hint says so when the condition fails.

Press Hint again and again and count how many turns it needs. Is it ever more than the number of red edges you started with?
